Fvery reader of Mrs Gaskell's delightful book " Cranford " will remember the de- licious picture of rural repose and village quaintness of character pourtrayed in that charming volume. Knutsford—it is need- less to say now-a-days—was the original of "Cranford," that Cheshire village having been once the country home of the dis- tinguished authoress In the following description of this sequestered home of Cheshire Quarter Sessions, the reader will discern a very different, but not less humor- ous rural picture.

In these rev, lutionary days a Court of Quarter &mons may be looked upon as a haven of rest. We put into one of these havens last week, and found ace. Con, ty town of Beechnut was tbe locus in quo ...curious old spot; principally cemposed of stables, as t seemed to us, and sequestered heaps of dung, which Were waiting to be "dug in" at a more convenient Season. A few of the habitants hung loosely about the one main street of Beechnut. who, in like manner with the ordure aforesaid, appeared to be waiting to bs is dug in," and to be qualifying for the same by the practice of inebriation meanwhile.

The Court el Quarter Sessions at Beechnut was held In a very highly respectable and prejudiced building a little out irf the town—just sufficiently out of it to make the inmates of the adjacent gaol feel cool and comfortable in their rotatory labours. The gaol stands somewhat hack fu cm the high road, and the Court. house projects from the gaol front. In honour of our institutions in Church and State, the parish church is ' cinvenient " to the prison—is, in fact, only separated from it by the high road. Date of the erection of the parish church not to be stated by the present writer. merely because h does not know what the date was The edifice itself appears to have anticipated the patio" of steam by lamming the construction of a brick locomotive crowned with nine-pine. The architect has no doubt long been gathered to his fathers, and if his lath. rs favoured the idiotic and strictly imbecile order of architecture, they will have welcomed this Wren of Beechnut with a round robin, who certainly, to judge from Beechnut Church, must have been the forerunner of the dry-earth closet. Having to visit Beechnut on public business, and at the expense of the public, we inquired very naturally what was the beet public to put up at. One of the in* habitants near the church gates—who was apparently choosing his last resting place in the company of a dog ...kindly pointed out the "Ring o' as, in a general way, "not to be beat." But or this anon. Close to the Court-house a concourse of persons wa- gathered together waiting for the real business or Quarter Session to begin. There had been an unusua• delay on this particular occasion on account of thc 'mush of Justices, who had assembled in such number' that they got mixed up with ordinary individuals and could with difficulty be identified. Two valuable pieces of eounty preferment had to be given away— the public "pig-killer," salary £5OO a-year and pig- quisites ; and that of the "hedger and ditcher," MP a-year and a horse—the horse being ready for him, and standing as much at ease as he could on the stretch of greensward outside the Court-house. Lounging on the read—preparatory to .the hard swearing of their calling—many members of the county police might be seen wi h the naked eye. They had that variety of waist which has always seemed to us to render police tailoring a very precarious vocatien. Nevertheless , they were many and not altogether devoid of thirst. Their somewhat pewt-r decorations, in respect of but- tons, led them to seek relief for their noses in the same preee us metal. Timid women went up to them and asked the roost jackass questions in the hope that their fri nds, shortly to appear in the dock, would inciden- tally derive advantage from the meciation of "the force," Liveried servants, with hats relieved from tedium by the smokejack of the aristocracy, paced up and down obedient to the wink of their masters. By- and-by a bevy of Justices came out, one of whom in- formed tie that his protele, Bellmetal, had been elected "pig-killer " to the county; likewise that a new Justice had just qualified from Stalebruck, I and that a few of them were about to his them to the " Ring o' bell" for the purpose of wetting his head. Having taken a calm and impartial survey of the udw Justice, and particularly of his head, we came to the conclusion that any moaerate degree of moisture would not seriously impair hi reasoning or juoicial faculties. This was about 2 p.m. Four hours later we vieited the Ring o' Bells" for the purpose of obtaining a toothpick, when we found the county Justices still pursuing the moistening process—their new brother, however, exhibiting symptoms by that time of perma- nent petrifaction. His Stony judicial outLok we shall nOt eainly forget; he seemed to be closing his eyes to everything but the point at issue, and to be fixing a jury in his mind's eye, to the lascivious pleasing of an jEolian harp. As the landlady said that she was out of toothpicks, we toothed a Scotch whisky instead, and returned to the court upon public business. By that time the ' appeat "in which we were interested had been called on, and tome twenty or thirty magistrates were pretending to hear with that mild inanity proper to the amateur jtu isprudence of Great Britain. Lrd Buttermilk, the chairman proper, had been properly sui,eri-eded in the function of trying appeals, and a barrister as deputy reigned in hip stead. Nevertheless, e noble Lord bobbed about on the bench in a carton, ly white hat, worn very mu i h in his neckhole. and exhibiting a marked reluctance to let *alone else open his mouth. All the other magieti able blushed when he spoke to them; and after he had spoken to some of the ii, he made grimaces to himself, and appeared to be indt.l4ing in private coavertatiol. w, Is 1)1133031f as to the dameum lot with which t e was eta' ounded. We felt quite a pride in seeing our own magi& rates—that is, the J.P.'s from our neighbourhood—on the Se- eione bench. There were the Joiner family in full concourse—Gadsden Joiner, the father, the pride and pomp of our village, se well known and as w.dely respected as tee villtge pump ; Magellan Joiner, his eon ; also Boiler J. deer, brother to Gadsden, and his son, commonly called "Eyeglass Harry," by reason 1 his restricted vision ; also his brother, Shcrr ,ck Joiner—the old Joiners having the proud pre-eminence of breeding Justices for the constantly accumulating villainy of the . Tillage. The "bar," seated in a well-hole underneath the bench, displayed a field of innocuous horsehair— guise argent, so to speak. We had retained Anchises, Q.C., special, and a junior well stricken in years, to help the groat man. Neither of them appeared to us to know anything about the case Wh,ll they started, but they gradually heeled on to it, like a barge knocked by ce ma/we on to a beach, and did sail they had all the tan been making for it on true nead.ical principles. Opposed to us was Bully Bullfi, oh, of the Polar circuit and Cheeking sessions ; with him the Honourable Grampus Norval, whose nerves appeared to be regu- larly unstrung. Ihe wordy clangour commenced. It was all about the comparative stench of a cucumber frame and the Public Health Act of Anno Domini— It cost a heap of money, and did no good to any human being, except, perhaps, to Anchises, Q.C., to Bully Bullfinch, and to the honourable Grampus, whose , digestion it must have hopelessly impaired for many I a long day. But how about the ends of justice P That I Is an altogether unseemiy question at a Court of Quarter Sessions, holden at Beechnut or anywhere else.

The two requisites for any successful literary, effort are discovery and conquest; in other words one musk, either say what has not been said before, or, if it has surpass others in its mode of expression._ Zsiir,it is only in the most limited sense that either requisite can be applied to these letters. , I am trying to open up new ground to some of your readers for their sum. mer tours. The peninsula of the Lizard is well worth a week's stay; our available time being short, we only spent a couple of days there. A coach took us from Pal month to HeUtone. It is a small town of 4,00 inhabi: tants, and a good central place from which to radiate to the points of interest. There is a curious legend as to the origin of the nanie; but like many others of the same nature the story was invented to explain the name. A certain nameless individual is supposed to have been wandering over Cornwall with the stone that formed the entrance to Hades. During his pen- gritiations he was stopped by t. Wawa, who forced him to an encounter, and he dropped his little play- thing. It fell on this spot. We were told a frag- ment of it could be seen in the inn yard, but the inn- keeper setmed gather ashamed of imposing on our credulity.

A walk of 12 miles across an uninteresting country brought us to Lizard town, a village about a mile from the Point. It was evening when we arrived, but we could not resist visiting at once "the far-jutting head- land." We rested close to the famous lighthouses, on a precipitous rock 185 feet above the level of the rest. less waters. The day was the anniversary of the sight- ing of the Spanish Armada in 1588, and as the historic vi,ion looms on the horizon, there stands befure us a living witness of its doom, a veritable Bon of Spain. The young man's skin is olive, and his hair as black rt 3 jet, though some nine generations have passed away Risco his shipwrecked ancestor found there a home. "My name, sir, is Joie. Jose we pronounces it now, sir; my sister's name is Sidonia, she was name& after my grandmother." From farther enquiries we find that he was born and has spent his life at the Lizard, that he has been twice to Falmouth, and only once as far as Penzance—and what astonished us in a man who gut part of his living from the waters, for he often engaged in pilchard fishing—though he has bathed hundreds -oi times he can't swim. However, we secured him for our next day's expedition.

Perhaps one uf the beet ways of seeing the Lizards if the weather is fine, is to take a boat, as we did, and pull round to Mullion. One has thus all the advan. tags of the exquisite colouring of the rocks, in whico respect the Lizard scenery is unique. There is the dark serpentine, with streass of different coloured stones, here as smooth as glass, reflecting the light; there, breaking into j egged peaks. As we pulled round, on one of the brightest sunnieet days, we lost none of the rugged beauties ot the dark rocks. Rounding the Old Lizard, we go near the Black Stags and the Man-of- War Rucks. th. scene ot the wreck of a transport. The adjacent conact.,w is called Pistol Meadow, from the quantity of firearms there thrown on shore. It would be uninteresting to name. all the bold headlands, stream-washed chines, and hamlets nestling in the 1 rocks. To your readers they would be unmeaning names, to one who has keen there, they recall aa lovely a bit of wrest scenery as can be found on England's shores, And oh the beauties of Kynance We lingered in the cove, reluctant to lose any of its retir. ing loveliness. It can hardly be described—it can be thoroughly enjoyed. " We looked up to the sky, :whose floating glow Spread like a rosy ocean vast and bright; We gazed upon the glittering Bea below, We heard the waves splash, and the wind so low." Finding a retired little sandy creek, and the day beig very hot, we bathed. During this pleasant operations we heard the boatman's voice—" I see a hawk's nest," and very soon after we saw him clambering over the smooth, hard, steep rock, to the great danger of his neck. The hawks were just fledged, and one took his first exercise by tumbling on the beach. Him we secured; .Farther on, near the Smuggler's Cave, the same boatman, who seemed himself to have the eye of a hawk, spied a young cormorant falling down the precipitous hill side. It was evidently descending faster than it intended. We pulled our boat into a long narrow opening, forming a cul-de-sac, with the walls rising almost perpendicularly from the water's edge. •We were forced to guide the boat with our hands on the rocky sides. When we approached the young bird I attompted to seize it, but instinctively, though it was plainly the first time it had touched the ,water, it immediately dived. Whim it rose, however, It was caught, and now both the Cormorant and the hawk are in Warrington, trophies from Kynance.

Will you go to the Post-office and the Devils bel- lows P said our guide. Toe names excited our curiosity, and we pulled to a small island called Aspara- gus island from the abundance of asparagus opinalis grown on it. There we found the rock was pierced by a deep fissure, through which at times a jet of water is thrown with a tremendous roar. A smaller hole will take in, from a strong current of air, pieces of paper or a pocket handkerchief. The usual explanation is ths. it is caused by compressed air, but how the air becomes , compressed, or how it gets there at all we were not told. The roar was very small for us, in fact iL roared like any sucking dove"; but we couli quite conceive how in stormy weather it might be very im- pning. the .Rill a bold headland, and the Soci,Rosk, so called because the serpentine there ex- h. b,t tLick lodes of steatite for.,.eq ly much used in po,te, y work, further on the lot ty Pradeasek and the Gull Rock, on all of which there were huedreds and tuousands of sea birds, we arrived at Mullion Cove. Here we left our boat, walked about a mile, and par- took at the lowly village Mu of a lunch of bread and cheese, which after our hard work tasted sweeter than the finest dinner one could get at the Lion or the Patte. arms, flr Tames est optimum condimentum, W .ion my boy translated," When you're hungry any- t is geol." A meeting of representatives of the various trads (societies of the town, to consider peace principles, called by the Liverpool Workmen's Peace Association, was held on Friday evening. KIMBLE moved—" That this meeting expresses its profound interest in the I,resent aspects of humanity throughout the world, but especially in the East and South Eastern Europe, and prays Almighty God to raise.up earnest men who shall go forth In-flis name and preach the Gospel to the poor, down-trod- den, and the misguided." The first part of the resolu- tion brought before them one ot the great aims assuredly that a missionary meeting had, namely, to deepen in their hearts the sense that by the very terms of their union to the Lord Jeri s, they were bound to cultivate and express a profound interest in humanity, the more so, peittaps, because they had found lately that the world had been abused. (Hear, hear.) But though the world had been so much abused. they could not afford to suffer themselves to be robbed of it. (Hear, hear.) Of all assembles, an assembly for the promotion of the work of the Christian Church—the mission work—and surely that was the whole work of the Christian Church—a meeting like that had for its aim the deepening, the intensifying, and the increasing of their sympathies with humanity. The two last terms of the resolution—"down-trodden" and "misguided" —had come before them very much lately. While they showed their Christian Sympathy with and sent the Gospel to the down-trodden, they should not for- got the misguided. They felt indignant at the acts of the misguided, but they should riot let their indigna- tion overcome the deeper and stronger sympathy of a Christian heart for those who had erred for want of knowledge. Therefore, it was part of their duty, net only to think of the down-tr ' ,dden but also at the same time to let their prayers go to the Lord that the misguided might he led to the truth. (Applause.)

(Applause.) The Rev. IL STENISNSON seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation, and the proceedings terminated.

div.p: GREAT HOTEL ROBBERY ,AT WIDNES.

Late on .Ssfarday evening a robbery of an extensive_ character was perpetrated at the Arch Hotel, Widnes, kept by Mr. Win. Groom. While the ~ proprietor and . . his family were busily engaged in the lower part of the house, seine - thieves, wh3 were evidently well acquainted with the habits of the family, obtained a ladder from an adjoining builder's yard, and gaining access to the landlord's bedroom, succeeded in carry • lag away a cashbox containing £BOO in gold and notes. In the chest from which the cashbox was abstracted was also a large bowl of silver, but this the thieves left behind, evidently well satir fled with the booty they had obtained alre,dy: The theft was not discovered until Mr. Groom and his wife were retiring to rot, and their gtief and dismay st their loss may easily be imagined As the money is chiefly in gold, it is feared that the thieves will be able to avoid detection. Toe police are making inquiries into the circumstances of the rob- bery, but as yet with no satisfactory result. • AN APPREHENSION.

Great excitement still prevails in Widnes respecting the recent burglary and robbery of money. The amount stolen a ppeais to have been somewhat over- estimated, a police notice, issued by Mr. Superinten- dent Brindle, stating that the cash-box contained £660 in sovereigns and half-sovereigns, in addition to a brewer's small account book, and that it was placed inside a clothes box in one of the bedrooms, which was forced open. A reward of £2O has been offered for in. formation, which may lead to the detection of the thieves; and on Monday evening, Mr. Inspector Bar- nett and Sergeant Townsend, acting on the receipt of information, apprehended a man who gave the name of Martin Ryan, and who states that he has no fixed place of abode; although he was then lodging in a house in Queen-street, Widnes. The man represented that he had no money, but upon being searched he was found to have three £6 Bank of England notes— numbered respectively 28046, 66677, and 02226—a quarter American dollar, two gold-plated sleeve links, three gold-plated shirt studs, and a deposit given by Yates and Co., Exchange Office and Bank, 37, Castle. street, Liverpool, in favour of Martin Ryan, for five 100 dollar bends, United States Funded Loan. He says that he has been in America seven years, and that he returned in August last, and has not worked since, but has lodged in cemmon lodging-houses in Liverpool and Runcorn. An extraordinary ease of attempted murder came before the Widnes magistrates, on Tuesday, when Joseph Ford a pilot, and his two sons, John Ford and Wm. H. Ford, surrendered to their bail on a charge of attempting to murder a rival pilot named Thos. Ogden, residing at Widnes. Mr. Husband prosecuted, and Mr Swift defended. From the evidence of the prosecutor it appeared that on the night of the Ist inst., he was on the pierhead at Widnes, looking out for boats to pilot, when the three prisoners came up, and the eldest son said " Now you b— we will have your life." He leaped into his boat, unshipped her from her moorings, and paddled his boat into the sea. The three prisoners instantly gave chase in their own boat, and each seizing an oar rapidly followed him. Knowing that he could not swim he made for the shore, and was again fol- lowed by the prisoners, who leaped out of their boat and chased him on the bank. Seizing hold of him they knocked him down, and kicked him severely, finally throwing him head first into a mud pit, filled with filth about ten feet deep. In spite of his cries, the prisoners left him in the pit and returned to their boat. After some time he managed to crawl out of the hole. From the injuries he had received he bled profusely, and upon getting out and reaching his lodgings, his land- lady did not know him, so altered was hie appearance. He bled for five days, from his nose and his month after the assault, and was unable to follow his employ- ment. One of the witnesses was a lock-keeper, and the next morning after the outrage, he saw him, but , failed to recognise him his face was BO terribly dis- figured. For the defence it was urged that there had been a stand up tight between the prisoners and the prosecutor, and that no murder had been intended. oL Blackburne, M.P. said the bench was of opinion that the prosecutor had been most savagely assaulted, and they had determined to send the prisoners for trial to the sessions, The prisoners were then corn- mated to girkdale Sessions.

He Bail he understood that that was a meeting of the electors of Lowerhouse Ward in Burnley—(hear, hear) —and it was only an accidental circumstance that a meeting which really belonged to a part of Burnley was being held outside the borough in the township of Padiham. It was simply in consequence of the committee of the Lowerhouse district being unable to get a convenient room for holding their meeting in that district, and therefore they thought that as Padi- ham was so near to Lowerhouse they might venture to migrate to Padiham and hold their Burnley Lowerhouse meeting within that township. Under ordinary circumstances in addressing bis Burnley constituents at the close of the parliamentary session, he should no deubt have referred to and passed in review the various proceedings of the Government during the past session, and if he had taken that as his subject he could have shown them that the conduct of the Government had been marked both by inefficiency and extravagance. But he did not intend to go into that matter that night. He might also go into questions in which the Liberal party were interested; he could go into the land quee- tion, the Church question, or the question of the exten- sion of the county franchise. ("We want that in Padiham.") Upon all those questions we had a great work before us as Liberals, and we intended to do it. (Hear, hear.) We did not believe that because we happened to be defeated in the election of 1874 the work of the Liberal party had come to an end. (" No, no.") We knew perfectly well that while it might have been a very unfortunate circumstance that the Tory party should go into power, and inflict upon this country for a period of years great expenditure and great burdens, and perhaps discredit the policy of this country in the eyes of the world, still there were some compensating advantages, because the people were learning from day to day how hollow and weak the imposture is that is presided vest by Benjamin Disraeli. (Applause.) He did not intend to dwell either upon circumstances of the past session, nor did he intend to go into.those important questions which sooner or later we, as the Liberal party, would have to deal with. We were at present in the midst of a great crisis, a great struggle oetween the Ministers and the public opinion of the country —(hear, hear)—and he could not feel that he would he right in a ddresieng a number of his fellow-countrymen if he did not take the opportunity of assisting, so far as he could, in that struggle, by means of which we were seeking to con- trol our Government, which, we believed, was taking a course disastrous to the credit of the country and degrading to our position in this enlightened age (Hear, hear.) He might say in passing that the people of Padiham had already had a meeting upon tins question, and had passed res dutions condemnatory ot the action of the Government; and he was glad to know that his most excellent and honourable friend— ha meant their neighboar, Mr. Ughtred Kay-Shuttles worth—attended the meeting in that place in order to , assist in an expression of opieeon on that subject on the part of the inhabitants of Padiham. (Hear, hear.) He wished to take up, in the first instance, a challenge which had been thrown down by one of the members of the Government, which challenge, he thought, was an insult to the people of this countay—be Mailed to the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer at Edinburgh. There had been many speeches inaie by members of the Gov, rnment, to all of which cry serious exceptions ceuld b teken ; but the statement which was made by Sir Stafford Northcote, who was a statesman of very great respectability —a m an who ' would not very willingly say what he did not believe— was, in fact, an insult and a discredit to the people of this nation. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said at Edinburgh in reference to this Eastern Question, "In reg ad to the general attitude which the people of Eegland hold with regard to the foreign policy of the Gevernrc ent, I may say that as a rule they don't un- derstand it." (Groans, and "Oh. oh.") If they did not understand it they paid for it. (Laughter and ap- plause.) Li order to carry out the foreign policy of the British Government at the beginning of this cen- tury, nundreda of millions of money had been spent, and hundreds of thousands of lives sacrificed, and fifer we had suffered this loss we hat the satisfaction, on the defeat of the great Napoleon, of meeting the other powers on the Continent and joieing together in the great treaty, which was called the treaty of Vienna. The people of England got that treaty in return for a debt which was now weighing upon every person in that assembly; £800,000,0e0 of debt piled round the shoulders of this country aud hung like a miilstone round our necks. The interest of that money had had to come out Of our sinews and labour, and what had we got for it? We got the treaty of Vienna in 1815: that was made mainly to keep the family of Napoleon Bonaparte from the throne of France. In a very few years the late Napoleon came to England and kissed tee cheek of the Queen of England, which was one departure from the Treaty of Vienna. The treaty was broken in various ways, and we were worse off through that for which we had paid so much than we other- wise should have been. We had nothing to show for that debt of blood, and there was nothing in the Treaty of Vienna which determined the State of Europe or the condition of European Powers. div.p: SATURDAY, OCTOBER 28, 1876.

A Conservative carnival is being held in Manchester, in celebration of the opening of a xapw Conservative Club. Carnivals are always melancholy, even in the congenial climates of Paris, /tome, and Venice, but a carnival in the smoky city of 'Blanchester, and a Conservative carnival besides, is such an appalling spectacle, that one is almost silenced by the pageant, and one's voice is hushed by the gigantic, solemn stupidity of the festival. 'lhe chief gaieties at this par- ticular carnival are conferences at which dull speeches are made, banquets at which bucolic toasts are drunk with rapture, and balls at which, we may surmise, Conservative love- making is carried on with decorum. The programme is a varied one in one sense, but in one sense only. Eating, drinking, and da cing are varied occupations, but they are apt to assume a somewhat monotonous character if they are always accompanied by the perpetual ding-dong of Conservative speeches. Whether the Tories meet to guzzle or to dance, the same awful Nemesis seems to be always in attendance either in the form of prolix members of Parliament or , else of those still more prolix persons, who, having unsuccessfully contested past elec- tions are anxious to explain the reasons of their defeat. We are indebted to the Man- chester Courier for a very full report of the sports, as far as they have gone, and we propose to pluck a few flowers from the rhetorical jungle, for the benefit of people who either do not see this newspaper, or who avoid its a matter of taste._ _

On Wednesday morning, Earl Stanhope presided at the Manchester Town liall, over a body of gentlemen who call themselves a ..,.ational Union. Apart from the modesty of the title, it is curious to observe that " among-t those present, were 1301310 of the L ast honoured of Manchester politicians, and it is very honest on the part of the Courier to record their names, when it might have suppressed them. Besides the gentle- men who constitute this National Union of Tooley-street, a number of delegates from Conservative and Constitutional Associations were present, and all their names are printed in full. Mr. Henry Gartside, of Ashton- under-Lyne, opened the proceedings by saying; "Before the report is read I should like to call the attention of the meeting to the fact that this is a conference of Conser- vative Associations." If the gentlemen present, being a little demoralized by the political dissipation of the week, did not know whether it was the ball, the banquet, or the conference, that they were attending it was only courteous on the part of Mr. Henry Gartside, of Ashton-under-Lyne, to inform them. But Mr. .Gartside gave a still more signal illustration of his tact and shrewdnesss, for he proposed that newspaper reporters should be ejected from the meeting, and but for the interference of the other National Unionists, we should be without the report from which we make the following extracts :—Mr. H. C. Raikes, M P., was of the opinion that it would not look well to suspect the dangers of publicity and he said " iteporters had attended all the conferences that had hitherto been held in connection with that organisation, and if the representatives of the press were ex- cluded from the present Conference, it might be supposed out of doors that the progress of Conservative associations during the past year had not been such as to make it desir- able that publicity sh,uld be given to it." 'Well! Ihe gentlemen of the press were ultimately permitted to do their best and their worst with the meeting, and judging by the speeches which they have given to the country, it is difficult to discover that the world is one whit the better or the wiser for so much laborious oratory. Much of the time of the meeting was occupied by Mr. Gamble, Q. 0., perhaps one of the most con- spicuous political failures out of Parliament; and Mr. F. S. Powell, who was lately so signally beaten by Mr. Jacob Bright at Ma ichester, and whose advent before a constituency seems to be an omen of defeat. Mr. Gamble, Q.C., appears as the very genius of commonplace. He s Aid "During the last two months the affairs of the country had brought home to their minds some very important facts. Tuey had shown them that the popular mind if neglected by the Conservative leaders might on certain occasions be so agi ated and carried away as to iuflict grievous damage upon the country. It had been shown that this mov- ing wave of popular opinion required to be continually guided and directed in a proper channel, and that if abandoned by those who were at t. e head of affairs and left subject to the exciting speeches and fervent eloquence of designing agitation or mis- guided statesmen it might be led in a direc- tion fraught with the most grievous conse- quences to the country." Mr. Gamble was further of opinion that "if the Conservative Associations of the country were only main- tained with vigor and energy the Conserva- tives would long remain in power, and not only that, but the country would be saved from danger and revolution." The public has been long familiar with Mr. Gamble's antiquated story. The Con- servative party is always saving the country from danger and revolution, and the Con- servative leaders are being always besought not to "neglect the popular mind," which is so liable to be agitated and carried away, and inflict grievous damage upon the coun- try. We all know the proper channel into' which gentlemen with Mr. Gamble's profes- sional and other aspirations, desire popular opinion to be continually guided and direc- ted. It is to drivel like this that annual meetings of Conservative and constitutional associations assemble to listen in Manches- ter and elsewhere, and it is to such demon- stration!, that the Tory party are pleased to attribute the continued existence of a ministry which dare not meet the constituen- cies which have bestowed upon them their mechanical majority, or to meet a Parlia- ment which they proclaim to be ready to sanction their policy in the East.
